articles.title: The Harness as the Only Mutable Surface: Compliance-Bounded Self-Evolution of LLM Agents in Credit Pipelines, with a Measured Admission Gate
articles.description:
arXiv:2610.10629v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents can adapt a credit pipeline to a changed rule, but an agent that rewrites itself destroys the artefact a supervisor reviews: a named change, a recorded test, an approval. We argue that self-evolution is reviewable only if it is confined to the runtime harness (instruction text, tool-call logic and primitive composition) while model weights stay fixed, so that every adaptation is a diff with a cause and a test attached. articles.title_zh: The Harness as the Only Mutable Surface: Compliance-Bounded Self-Evolution of LLM Agents in Credit Pipelines, with a Measured Admission Gate

articles.title: Reading the Room: Foundations, Design, and Challenges of Normative Competence in LLMs
articles.description:
arXiv:2610.10906v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human communities are governed by normative systems: shared standards that produce \textit{norms} dictating acceptable behavior, enforced through community sanctioning. articles.title: On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents
articles.description:
arXiv:2610.10833v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study whether small LLM agents can operate effectively under explicit wall-clock time budgets by both respecting the allocated runtime and using available time productively. We evaluate Qwen3.6-27B on five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Qwen3-4B on Zork I (Jericho), two agentic benchmarks where additional computational time can meaningfully improve performance. articles.title: Verification and Self-Improvement in Agentic AI: Foundations and Limits
articles.description:
arXiv:2610.10611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems can improve by searching longer, receiving additional support, or modifying how they propose and verify outputs. articles.title: How Narrative Wrapping Affects LLM Refusal: A Cross-Language Benchmark and Defense
articles.description:
arXiv:2610.11005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety-aligned language models often refuse a harmful request stated directly but answer the same request inside a role-play or narrative wrapper. We measure this vulnerability across languages and registers: attack success on Qwen3-1.7B is already 89.4% in English and 93.0% in modern Chinese, and reaches 95.7% in Classical Chinese.
